beats.say: A New Mexico rancher rode out across his ranch, and found shiny wreckage scattered all over the ground.
beats.headline: WHAT CRASHED?
beats.short_title: What REALLY Crashed at Roswell? 👽 Case #3
beats.comment: What did you think crashed? 👽 aliens / 🎈 balloon
beats.bonus: Project Mogul's balloon trains carried microphones to listen for Soviet nuclear tests. The Air Force's reports came out in 1994 and 1997.
beats.caption: What really crashed at Roswell in 1947? The cover-up was real. The aliens weren't. What did you guess? 👽 aliens / 🎈 balloon #roswell #ufo #history #meatballinvestigates Follow Meatball for a new case every day 🍝
sources: US Air Force, 'The Roswell Report: Fact vs. Fiction in the New Mexico Desert' (1995) and 'The Roswell Report: Case Closed' (1997): the debris came from Project Mogul, a classified balloon train carrying sensors to detect Soviet nuclear tests; the 'alien body' stories were explained as anthropomorphic test dummies from 1950s high-altitude drops — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mogul (checked 2026-10-26)

Wikipedia, Roswell incident (rancher W. W. 'Mac' Brazel found debris in June-July 1947; 8 July 1947 RAAF press release announced a recovered 'flying disc'; the next day Gen. Roger Ramey said it was a weather balloon; interest revived in the late 1970s) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roswell_incident

beats.say: Foil, sticks, tape, rubber. So what really crashed? Guess.
Subscribe. I investigate a weird case every day.
See, in July 1947, the Army base at Roswell put out a press release. They said they'd recovered a flying disc.
The next day, a general posed with the pieces and said, never mind, it's a weather balloon.
Guess one: a flying saucer, and the bodies were hidden. That's what the books said decades later.
Guess two: a plain weather balloon, exactly what the Army said. That's not it either.
So I went to check Area 51 myself. Bad idea. They do not do tours.
Wait. Here's the weird part. The balloon story was a cover story too.
Verdict: a secret spy balloon. Project Mogul. A long train of balloons carrying microphones, to hear Soviet nuclear tests.
It was top secret, so nobody could say what it really was. For decades.
The Air Force finally explained it in 1994. Then came the alien bodies.
Their answer? Crash test dummies, dropped from the sky in the 1950s.
So the cover-up was real. The aliens weren't.
Did you guess right? Comment.
And the name of the Air Force's last report on it? Case Closed. It did not close the case.
America's top general signed a plan to blow up an American ship, and blame it on Cuba.

beats.headline: FAKE ATTACKS?
beats.short_title: Operation Northwoods: The Conspiracy That Was TRUE 🔍 Case #2
beats.comment: Did you know this was real? ✅ yes / 😳 no idea
beats.bonus: One idea in the plan: fake the shoot-down of a civilian airliner with a remote-controlled drone. The memo was declassified in 1997.
beats.caption: Operation Northwoods: the 1962 plan for fake attacks blamed on Cuba. Did they do it? ✅ yes / ❌ no #conspiracy #history #coldwar #declassified #meatballinvestigates Follow Meatball for a new case every day 🍝
sources: Joint Chiefs of Staff memorandum to the Secretary of Defense, 'Justification for US Military Intervention in Cuba', 13 March 1962 (Operation Northwoods), signed by Gen. L. L. Lemnitzer; includes 'We could blow up a US ship in Guantanamo Bay and blame Cuba' and a drone substituted for a civilian airliner — National Security Archive — https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/news/20010430/ (checked 2026-10-26)

Wikipedia, Operation Northwoods (rejected by the Kennedy administration; Kennedy did not reappoint Lemnitzer as Chairman, he became NATO's SACEUR in late 1962; declassified 1997 by the Assassination Records Review Board) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Northwoods
beats.loop_say: Always read the fine print. Because

beats.say: So, did they actually do it? Guess.
Subscribe. I investigate a weird case every day.
See, in March 1962, the Pentagon wanted a reason to invade Cuba. So the Joint Chiefs wrote one.
The memo listed fake attacks. Blow up a ship at Guantanamo. Stage a terror campaign in Miami.
Wait, it gets worse. Swap a passenger plane for a drone, and fake its shoot-down.
Guess one: they did it, and history got the blame wrong. No. None of these attacks happened.
Guess two: the memo is a forgery the internet made up. Also no.
So I asked for a copy. They stamped me CLASSIFIED.
Verdict: the memo is real. The top brass really proposed it, and Kennedy's team said no.
Months later, the general who signed it was moved out, to a job in Europe.

beats.short_title: The Dancing Plague of 1518 Was REAL 💃 Case #5
beats.comment: Could this happen today? 😬 yes / 🙅 no way
beats.bonus: It happened in Strasbourg in July 1518. The physician Paracelsus wrote about it a few years later.
beats.caption: The dancing plague of 1518 was real: people in Strasbourg danced for days, and the city hired a band. Could it happen today? 😬 yes / 🙅 no way #dancingplague #history #weirdhistory #meatballinvestigates Follow Meatball for a new case every day 🍝
sources: Wikipedia, Dancing plague of 1518 (Strasbourg, July 1518; began with one woman, Frau Troffea; dozens joined within a week, later accounts say up to about 400; authorities prescribed more dancing, opened guild halls, built a stage and hired musicians; dancers were later taken to a shrine of St. Vitus; leading explanation mass psychogenic illness amid famine and disease, ergot theory disputed) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_plague_of_1518 (checked 2026-10-26)
John Waller, 'A forgotten plague: making sense of dancing mania', The Lancet 373 (2009): 624-625 — https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60386-X
beats.loop_say: Never trust a catchy song. Because
beats.say: What if I told you that in 1518, a whole city caught a dancing plague, and people couldn't stop for days?
It's real. City records, doctors' notes, even a sermon. It started with one woman, in July.
Could something like this happen today? Vote.

beats.say: Subscribe. I open a new case every day.

shots.obs: wm:Die Wallfahrt der Fallsuechtigen nach Meulebeeck.jpg

beats.say: See, in July 1518, Strasbourg was starving. Bad harvests, freezing winters, sickness everywhere.
Then a woman stepped into the street and began to dance. No music. She didn't stop for days.
Within a week, dozens more had joined her. Later accounts say hundreds.
But here's the thing. The city leaders made it worse.

shots.obs: wm:Die Wallfahrt der Fallsuechtigen nach Meulebeeck.jpg

beats.say: Doctors said the cure was more dancing. So the city opened halls, built a stage, and hired a band.

shots.obs: wm:Die Wallfahrt der Fallsuechtigen nach Meulebeeck.jpg

beats.say: I read about it too long. Now my foot is tapping. Please send help.

shots.obs: wm:Die Wallfahrt der Fallsuechtigen nach Meulebeeck.jpg

beats.say: Some dancers reportedly collapsed from exhaustion. The city finally banned public dancing and music.
Today, most historians think it was mass panic, a stress illness that spread through a starving, frightened city.
The dancers were taken up a mountain to a saint's shrine, and given red shoes.

shots.obs: wm:Die Wallfahrt der Fallsuechtigen nach Meulebeeck.jpg

beats.say: What's your theory? Comment it.

The city's first cure for a dancing plague was a live band. Nobody checked who was booking the gigs.

beats.headline: NUKE THE MOON?
beats.short_title: The US Planned to Nuke the Moon. It's REAL 🌕 Case #4
beats.comment: Would you have pushed the button? 🌕 yes / 🚫 no
beats.bonus: The study, 'A Study of Lunar Research Flights' (AFSWC-TR-59-39, 1959), stayed secret for about 40 years. Carl Sagan worked out how the dust cloud would spread.
beats.caption: Did the US plan to nuke the Moon? Yes: Project A119, 1958. Would you have pushed the button? 🌕 yes / 🚫 no #coldwar #weirdhistory #space #meatballinvestigates Follow Meatball for a new case every day 🍝
sources: Wikipedia, Project A119 (US Air Force project carried out by the Armour Research Foundation at the Illinois Institute of Technology, Chicago, led by Leonard Reiffel; research began May 1958, cancelled January 1959; the blast was meant to be visible from Earth, partly to boost morale after Sputnik; Carl Sagan modelled the expansion of the dust cloud; revealed after Keay Davidson found Sagan had listed classified paper titles in his 1959 Miller Institute fellowship application) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_A119 (checked 2026-10-26)

L. Reiffel, 'A Study of Lunar Research Flights', Vol. I, Armour Research Foundation for the Air Force Special Weapons Center, 19 June 1959, AFSWC-TR-59-39, DTIC AD0425380 — https://apps.dtic.mil/sti/pdfs/AD0425380.pdf
Antony Barnett, The Observer, 14 May 2000 (Reiffel confirms the plan; the aim was a show of strength)
beats.say: What if I told you the US Air Force once studied how to set off a nuclear bomb on the Moon?
It's real. The project was called A119, and the plan was for people on Earth to see the flash.
Would you have pushed the button? Vote.
Subscribe. I open a new case every day.
See, in October 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik, the first satellite. Americans could watch it fly over their heads.
America felt like it was losing the space race. Badly. So the Air Force wanted something big.
In 1958, it quietly hired a lab in Chicago to study a lunar research flight. That was the polite name.
Wait. Here's the real goal. A bomb on the edge of the Moon, timed so the flash would be seen from Earth.
A show of strength, so the whole world could look up and see it.
The Moon is round and gray. So am I. I'm staying indoors.
A young scientist named Carl Sagan worked out how the dust cloud would spread.
Then, in January 1959, it was cancelled. People feared the fallout, and the backlash. It stayed secret for about forty years.
What's your theory: would it have worked? Comment it.
Follow Meatball. A new case every day.
How did the world find out? Sagan listed the secret papers on a job application. Great résumé.
